title: Story of an edtech startup in 2020–2: Takeaways
body_markdown:
Our experience in 2020 was not only about the rapid changes edtech encountered. This period, which was labeled by Sequoia in its infamous article,[Coronavirus: The Black Swan of 2020](https://medium.com/sequoia-capital/coronavirus-the-black-swan-of-2020-7c72bdeb9753) , required a paradigm shift for startups at every phase, in every industry.


In the early days of the pandemic, a different startup analogy began to be discussed more prominently —[being a camel rather than a unicorn](https://www.inc.com/jessica-stillman/why-more-startups-should-aim-to-be-camels-than-unicorns.html) . This shift was predominately inspired by successful startups outside the United States, and Silicon Valley more specifically. As startups all over the world began desperately seeking funding, certain principles we at Kunduz, an edtech startup operating in Turkey and India, have followed from the beginning helped us get through this difficult time more soundly and, more importantly, with better peace of mind.


These principles may not be as *sexy* as the ones in popular Medium articles out of Silicon Valley, but we have found them essential for building a long-lasting organization, especially in a startup ecosystem that does not have the continuous, generous investors often found in Silicon Valley.


### What are these principles?


#### 1. Be in control of your finances.


Let’s start with the most boring but *most* vital part. It is essential to acknowledge that startups that grow without any investment are rare for a reason. On the other hand, it is important for a startup to have a financial projection plan where the business is eventually able to take care of itself in a conservative scenario, ideally within 12 months — at most 18 months — *so you will not be as heavily dependent on the next rounds of investment if things don’t go as well as you planned.* That means developing a realistic scenario where your business is able to generate enough cash to sustain operations with only the cash you have left.


Paul Graham famously frames this as being “[default dead or alive](http://www.paulgraham.com/aord.html) ”. Are you *“default alive”* or *“default dead”* at any given moment? This is something every entrepreneur should know.


It is necessary to be careful about these issues from the beginning:


**🛰 Test your business model from day one —** With the right business model, your users will always be your biggest investor and reduce your dependence on venture investors. Selling at the right profitability will be even more valuable as you scale. Moreover, having a financially viable model is also the most honest test for product-market fit. Testing your financially viable business with users at the right price may result in harsh realities early on, but in the long run, these learnings will result in the biggest savings — of time, money, and stress.


🛰 **Think thrice before every expense** — Keep this mindset for the first 5 years, even after a new round of funding. $5,000 may seem like an insignificant cost when you look at your hefty cash balance now, but it may be vital should things go downhill 15 months later. This doesn’t necessarily mean you should be stingy. With every cost item you have for the company, you should evaluate both the value the business will receive and the opportunity cost for the business. Kunduz hasn’t provided any flashy team swag in the past 5 years and founders are using developers’ old laptops or are still using their own personal laptops. But that doesn’t mean we are not supporting our team members or providing great benefits. For us, these expenses have greatly lagged in priority when we compared the benefits and costs.


👓 Must-read: Paul Graham —[Default Alive or Default Dead?](http://www.paulgraham.com/aord.html#:~:text=If%20the%20company%20is%20default,the%20current%20trajectory%20ends%20badly.&text=But%20as%20the%20company%20grows,switches%20from%20meaningless%20to%20critical.)


Pre-Covid — A group from different teams produce Youtube video content for our content marketing tests. We have teammates from Product, Growth, Tutor Onboarding, and Customer Support teams pictured here.


#### 2. Learn as much about your users as you know about your best friend.


When we started Kunduz, one of the common denominators of our team was that we were all nerds at school. The founders were in the top 400 for the university entrance exam, which is taken by 2.5 million students. When recruiting, we were giving priority to the candidates who had previously been tutors at Kunduz for certain roles. We were trying to change something in a market where we were once power users. But, past experience may lose its usefulness in a changing market. So, we had to acknowledge that our prior experience was increasingly less relevant. This requires paying close attention to users in strategic and product decisions and never overlooking their needs. It should be applied in two forms:


🔦 **Constantly read your data** — Very strong evidence on a high scale for showing user behaviors, as opposed to solely listening to what users say. Although it is hard to draw meaningful results from data for a low-scale startup at an early stage, you can still derive valuable information, especially once the right scale is obtained. It can be less capable of giving you the causality you are looking for.


🔦 **Spend time with your users, probably more than you do with your family** — Spending time with your users and assimilating to their needs, preferences, and problems will help you contextualize inferences from the data or can provide valuable hints on what data to analyze if you don't know yet. There are many valid methods here, from the Five Whys to simple prototype testing. You can also find your own unique way that fits in the nature of your product.


An example of this is our MVP. Our first product only used a Whatsapp account. Students would send a question they needed help with to a number — which was Başar’s personal phone number. We managed to manually solve thousands of questions from this one account by sending the questions to Whatsapp groups we formed for tutors. Whoever solved the question first would earn the money — not so different from our flagship Q&A product.


We used this to test our hypothesis as quickly and as inexpensively as possible. From this, we learned way more than we intended to. Having spent so much time with our students and tutors at every moment of their product experience, we became friends with them and were able to deeply understand their needs, which has saved us a massive amount of time making decisions at every stage of scaling Kunduz. Additionally, once a year we allocate 1 week solely to interviews with users (in addition to the product team’s routine user interviews for every new feature).


👓 Must-read — Paul Graham —[Do Things That Don’t Scale](http://www.paulgraham.com/ds.html)


00:45


#### 3. Build a growth engine.


In the past 9 months, Kunduz has developed 4 new products all while still iterating on its flagship product. User adoption in edtech has been virtually turbocharged. Our users need new solutions now more than ever—which is exactly what every entrepreneur wants to hear.


There is a dilemma when starting to work on new products. On the one hand, you are diluting your focus by expanding your product offerings. On the other side, you are leveraging your user base by catering to more needs of your users with additional products and features. The best way to address this dilemma is to consider these two questions:


(1) *Do you honestly think that you have found a product-market fit that aligns with your core product?*


(2) *Do you have enough human resources to build new products and find product-market fits for them?*


You should only be working on new things if you can confidently say yes to both of these questions.


This mindset can be applied by focusing on only your core product too. Either way, the speed of development requires demonstrating two crucial strengths:


👩🏻‍🔬 **Prioritize user needs correctly** — We are already at a point where we understand users’ needs from spending time with them and analyzing the data. For prioritization, we have used the method advised by[Rahul Vohra from Superhuman](https://firstround.com/review/how-superhuman-built-an-engine-to-find-product-market-fit/) , who was inspired by Sean Ellis and his book, Hacking Growth. Every startup needs its own modification for this and it needs to evolve as the startup scales.[Onur Yavuz,](https://www.linkedin.com/in/onur-yavuz-94007628/?originalSubdomain=tr) Kunduz’s Head of Product, keeps iterating our own modifications so that we can continue to use them in more complex structures as we work on different products and markets with a larger team. Onur will be sharing more comprehensive articles on this topic on[Kunduz, Inc.](http://kunduzinc.medium.com/)


👩🏻‍🔬 **Build an A+ team** — We talked about the difference between cost-conscious and stingy. Recruitment is the best example of this distinction. The most important asset of a startup is time and the key factor that makes one successful is to maximize the work done in a limited time. The simplest way to achieve this is to establish a team that can deliver the fastest with the highest quality. A+ candidates can be costly for a startup but this is insignificant compared to the value and time you will gain from hiring top talent. As a result, important work falls on the founders beyond just allocating a hiring budget. This is a topic that deserves an article of its own, but here are a few quick hiring tips:


1. Spend 20% of your time meeting the best talent out there, even if you are not currently hiring. Hiring a candidate who is not a good fit for the team just because you need to recruit fast will cause a much greater waste of time in the long run. To get ahead of yourself, keep meeting talent throughout the year.
2. Interview people with top-notch experience and skillsets that you know you cannot afford. It will allow you to understand what it means to be perfect in any role —this has been invaluable advice that we heard from other YC founders.
3. The right candidate doesn’t have to be the most skilled candidate. Cultural fit becomes as important as the skillset.
4. The real candidate is you, not the person you interview. Be aware that none of these conversations are one-sided. Quite the contrary, your first role is to introduce your startup and yourself to the candidate in the best way possible. If you feel that they are excited about what you share, it means you are onto a potential long-term teammate who could be as motivated about the problem you are trying to solve as you are.


Must-reads:


👓 Rahul Vohra —[How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product/Market Fit](https://firstround.com/review/how-superhuman-built-an-engine-to-find-product-market-fit/)


👓 Josh Reeves —[How Gusto Built Scalable Hiring Practices Rooted in Tradition](https://firstround.com/review/how-gusto-built-scalable-hiring-practices-rooted-in-tradition/)


09:30


#### 4. Create a culture that keeps people happy and productive


If there is something more valuable than adding A+ members to your team, it’s being able to keep them on your team for many years to come.


This is another topic that deserves a separate article, but if there is one thing that should make leaders contemplate every decision, it is how to keep an A+ player happy and productive. Keeping an A+ teammate always takes much less effort than recruiting a new one.


The most important advice here is not a head-scratcher: Empathize with your team on decisions that will directly or indirectly impact them. Looking from someone else’s perspective is a strength that takes time to build, but can save you years.


Culture is something that should not be postponed. Our YC partner Tim Brady’s advice has stuck with us: The cultural DNA of a startup is what you do in the early days and is whom you hire as your first 20 employees. After that, it gets harder and harder to change things.


We also made some big mistakes here and learned this lesson the hard way. *At the time, those mistakes seemed like small decisions.*


The last thing you want to think about while working on a seemingly bigger — but inherently just more urgent — problem, likely on only a few hours of sleep, is the culture of your startup, but we assure you that you will owe your sleep to it in a few months.


20:15


These principles may seem a little too romantic, but each one is a decision that will impact you financially. The time you spend with your users will help you understand them better and prevent you from investing in the wrong direction for your business *or* your startup’s culture will help your team last longer.


While we are influenced by our personal experiences at Kunduz, we tried to share our learnings from a universal point of view. The examples here come from our story. Of course, you don’t have to follow every word verbatim. You might work in biotech and your product requires extensive funding for its 3-year research study or maybe your company should really buy you a laptop.


None of these principles that we have applied are new. We have accumulated them thanks to the books we read, the YC community, and the generous people of the World Wide Web. We filtered them for our own ambitions and struggles. We don’t see any reason why they would be irrelevant to any entrepreneur, especially those operating in a non-Silicon Valley world.


Throughout 2021, the Kunduz team will continue to publish articles on entrepreneurial topics via our[Medium publication](http://medium.com/kunduzinc) . We cannot wait to share more about Kunduz — our experiences, gains, and mistakes of this journey with people like you, whether you have your own startup or are a future entrepreneur.


You can reach us atfounders@kunduz.com with your questions and suggestions.


Wish you all a better year than the last 🎢


Barış, Başar & Melih
